title: Cauchy, with nowhere to go

prereqs.why: The example has to be Cauchy, which is a condition on the terms and not on a limit.
The point of the example is that completeness is a property of the space.
The same sequence of numbers is convergent in one space and not in another.

statement:
**Claim.** *In any metric space, every Cauchy sequence converges.*

This is false, and the usual counterexample lives in the space

$$X = (0, 1] \quad\text{with}\quad d(x,y) = |x-y|.$$

Build the standard counterexample by giving three terms of a sequence $x_n = 1/n$ and the number it is trying to converge to.

The sequence $1/n$ is Cauchy — its terms get arbitrarily close to each other — but the point it approaches has been removed from the space.
hints: Cauchy is a condition on pairs of *terms*: for every $\eps$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n) < \eps$ whenever $m,n \ge N$. Notice it never mentions a limit.
The sequence $1/n$ is $1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac14, \dots$. Every one of those is in $(0,1]$. Where is it heading?
It is heading for $0$ — and $0$ is not in $X$. That is the whole counterexample: nothing in the space is close to all the late terms.

payload.claim: In any metric space, every Cauchy sequence converges.
payload.guidance: Fill in three terms of $x_n = 1/n$ and the value it approaches in $\R$. The checker will confirm the terms really are $1/n$, that they are distinct, and that the limit lies outside $X = (0,1]$.

fields.label: The tenth term, $x_{10}$
fields.syntax: A number or a fraction. 1/10 and 0.1 are the same answer.
